result:
There's something strangely comforting about the sound of rain on a window when you're warm and dry inside. It's a reminder that the world is still turning, still doing its ancient weather routines, completely indifferent to our deadlines and anxieties. The clouds don't care about your inbox. The thunder doesn't have a performance review next Thursday.

I think about how much energy we spend worrying about things that haven't happened yet. We rehearse arguments in the shower with people who aren't there. We draft emails in our heads at 2 AM. We catastrophize so beautifully and so efficiently that we practically deserve awards for it. Meanwhile, the actual present moment — the one we're always trying to get past on our way to the next thing — keeps asking for attention and receiving none.

What would it be like to live more like a tree? Roots deep, branches open, weathered by everything but rooted to the spot regardless. Trees don't sprint toward their goals. They just grow, one slow ring at a time, and somehow they still reach the sky.

I don't mean we should do nothing. Movement is beautiful. Ambition has its own grace. But maybe there's wisdom in pausing long enough to notice that you are already somewhere, already breathing, already here. The rain will stop eventually. And when it does, everything outside will smell like clean earth and possibility.

Sometimes that's enough.
